section_summary: This section covers the internal political developments and cabinet reorganizations in wartime Japan from early 1942 through late 1944, focusing on the crisis and ultimate collapse of Premier Hideki Tojo's administration. It details Tojo's February 1944 cabinet and military command reshuffles following setbacks at Truk, as well as the fall of his government in July 1944 after the catastrophic loss of Saipan. The documents analyze the formation of the successor Koiso-Yonai Cabinet, its efforts to broaden political and industrial support for continuing the war, and subsequent military and Privy Council appointments reported by U.S. and foreign diplomatic missions.

subfiles.about: Continuation of a telegram from Bern reporting German press coverage and interpretation of Premier Tojo's cabinet reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Bern report: Transport Minister Goto will revitalize transport organizations; German press, citing Tojo's adjustments, sees centralized authority, faster production and a united front for victory.
subfiles.title: German Press Reaction to Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a report received from Argentina concerning the Greater East Asia Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a confidential report (Despatch No. 13993, February 25, 1944) from Argentina on the Greater East Asia Ministry (701.0090/3582).
subfiles.title: Report on Greater East Asia Ministry Submitted

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing the February 1944 Japanese Cabinet changes and senior military staff dismissals following defeats at Truk.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Tojo appointed Ishiwatari, Uchida and Goto as ministers, civilian nationalists to placate business; after Truk losses Sugiyama and Nagano were relieved, with Tojo and Shimada taking the General Staff posts.
subfiles.title: Recent Japanese Political Changes

subfiles.about: Detailed memorandum examining the biographical backgrounds and political implications of ministerial changes in the Tojo Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Benninghoff details the February 19, 1944 cabinet replacements (Ishiwatari, Uchida, Goto) and profiles them: Tojo is shifting to civilian figures for war production, but defeats could unseat him.
subfiles.title: Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Memorandum transmitting an intercepted FCC broadcast report on the inaugural installation of the Japanese-sponsored Philippine Executive Commission in Manila.
subfiles.summary: FCC interception of January 27, 1942 on the occupation government in Manila; annotations identify Vargas, Aquino, de las Alas, Laurel and others.
subfiles.title: FCC Monitoring Service Report on the New Philippine Government

subfiles.about: Telegram from Bern analyzing the political significance of Admiral Naokuni Nomura's appointment as Japanese Navy Minister.
subfiles.summary: Bern telegram: Admiral Naokuni Nomura, formerly Naval Attaché in Berlin and Tripartite Pact negotiator, becomes Navy Minister, putting a German-experienced officer at the Navy's head.
subfiles.title: Appointment of Admiral Nomura as Japanese Naval Minister

subfiles.about: Memorandum reporting the en bloc resignation of the Tojo Cabinet following the loss of Saipan and the imperial command to form a new government.
subfiles.summary: Dickover: the Tojo Cabinet resigned en bloc July 18, 1944, over Saipan; the Emperor told Yonai and Koiso to form a successor. The change reflects military weakness, not willingness to abandon the war.
subfiles.title: Japan: Resignation of Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Preliminary memorandum evaluating the structure and ministerial appointments of the newly established Koiso-Yonai Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: First observations on the Koiso-Yonai Cabinet: power no longer concentrated in Tojo, Ogata at the Board of Information, and Shigemitsu holding Greater East Asia Affairs; a broader base committed to the war.
subfiles.title: Japan: New Cabinet

subfiles.about: State Department press release warning against false optimism following the resignation of the Tojo Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew's public statement: the Tojo Cabinet's resignation admits military defeats and bolsters morale, but Japan will fight to the end and the military dictatorship remains.
subfiles.title: Statement by the Honorable Joseph C. Grew on the Resignation of the Tojo Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a dispatch from Ceylon regarding the resignation of the Tojo Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a July 22, 1944 communication from Ceylon (894.00/7-2244) on the Tojo Cabinet's resignation.
subfiles.title: Resignation of the Tojo Cabinet in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive memorandum with attached biographical register analyzing the fall of the Tojo Cabinet and the composition of the Koiso Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: A transmittal note from Johansen presents a detailed analytical study and comprehensive biographical register regarding the fall of the Tojo government and the formation of the Koiso-Yonai Cabinet. The memorandum traces Tojo's maneuvers to preserve power prior to the en bloc resignation on July 18, 1944, which was forced by the disastrous fall of Saipan and domestic discontent over his dictatorial unification of civil and military command. It concludes that the Koiso Cabinet was organized not to seek peace, but to invigorate the war effort by assembling experienced administrators, party figures, industrialists, and press representatives. The accompanying seven-page biographical appendix details the careers of outgoing and incoming ministers across all major portfolios.
subfiles.title: Change in Government (with Sketches of Members of Tojo and Koiso Cabinets)

subfiles.about: Telegram from Moscow quoting Soviet press coverage of Domei dispatches on the formation of the Koiso-Yonai Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Harriman forwards a Domei report that Koiso and Yonai are jointly organizing the new cabinet.
subfiles.title: Progress of Cabinet Formation under Koiso and Yonai

subfiles.about: Telegram from Moscow translating Soviet press reports of Japanese military transfers affecting Tojo, Yonai, Koda, and Sugiyama.
subfiles.summary: Harriman reports Tojo moved to the reserve, Yonai returned to active duty as Navy Minister, and Koda succeeded Sugiyama as Chief Inspector of Military Instruction.
subfiles.title: Japanese War Ministry Announcements on Military Appointments

subfiles.about: Telegram from Moscow reporting the appointment of Admiral Suzuki as President and Toru Shimizu as Vice President of the Privy Council.
subfiles.summary: Harriman reports Admiral Suzuki became Privy Council president after Hara's death on August 7, 1944, and Shimizu became vice president.
subfiles.title: Leadership Changes in the Japanese Privy Council

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a State Department memorandum concerning the resignation of the Japanese Minister of Munitions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Gullgren's December 20, 1944 memorandum on the Minister of Munitions' resignation (740.0011 P.W./12-2044).
subfiles.title: Resignation of the Minister of Munitions in the Japanese Government
